newsitem.title: DENMARK: Copenhagen futures market fights to boost turnover.
newsitem.headline: Copenhagen futures market fights to boost turnover.

text.p: Denmark's Futop futures and options exchange cut losses and increased turnover in 1996 compared to 1995 but is still far short of 1994's trade and fighting to improve, managing director Tyge Vorstrup Rasmussen told Reuters on Thursday.
Turnover edged up to 747,723 contracts in 1996 from 714,024 the year before, while the exchange's losses after tax fell to 9.8 million crowns from 1995's shortfall of 19.3 million.
The 1996 turnover comprised 349,846 interest rate-based contracts and 397,877 based on shares.
Total average daily turnover was 2,991 contracts, a far cry from 1994's 5,708.

"We have had weak turnover for the past two years. Some of the decline is probably due to the Barings scandal but we don't fully know what the reason is," Rasmussen said after a briefing on the market.
He said that the January 1, 1997, merger with the Copenhagen Stock Exchange would cut FUTOP overheads and should increase turnover by creating a unified Danish market for derivatives.
New products and streamlined procedures had been introduced, he added.
Trade could be boosted further if rules governing institutional investors' dealings were relaxed, he said.
Rasmussen estimated that roughly half of FUTOP trades were currently executed by foreign investors but that liquidity would have to grow to attract more foreign players.
FUTOP executives have spoken in the past of a possible alliance with a foreign partner -- London's LIFFE and the Stockholm OM markets have been mentioned as prospects.
Rasmussen said that now Futop was a wholly-owned subsidiary of the stock exchange the bourse board would have to decide on any future overseas partnership.

Panellists from different sides of the industry mainly agreed that while major professional users such as the leading banks were perfectly at home with futures and options, using them as a common tool, brokers needed to educate other potential users.

"There is nothing wrong with futures and options, but there is something wrong with customers buying products that they do not understand and of which they can not therefore calculate the risks," Klaus Struwe, of the stockbrokers' association said.
"There are some adults who still believe in Santa Claus and think that they can make huge profits with no risk," he added.
